title: Heritage Foundation: School Choice Is Wokeness Antidote
author: Peter Greene
summary: Greene takes apart a Heritage Foundation report claiming that school choice reduces wokeism in education. He argues it is a culture-war opinion piece dressed in research clothing: its footnotes mostly link to other opinion outlets, and it frames the issue as an empirically testable claim. Its method counts eight keywords in the handbooks of the largest charters in each state and correlates the count with a state charter-regulation score. The report gathers no data on public schools, so the comparison it claims to make is never made. Greene concludes that this is an argument for deregulating charters and defunding public education, and that presenting it as science is intellectually dishonest. The piece is a worked example of how to read advocacy research critically.
points: Greene argues the report's footnotes mostly point to other opinion pieces, so the research costume has little evidence underneath.
The wokeness measure, a count of eight words in charter handbooks, is a weak proxy, and the authors never define the term.
The study collects no public school data, so it cannot show that charters are less woke than public schools.
He reads the report as a strategic effort to harness the culture wars for deregulating charters and reducing public education funding.
quotes: Greene argued that the culture wars were an opportunity that choicers "should not squander.
The report has an academic research costume on, but it is something else. And we catch a whiff right in the first lurid paragraph.

They measured how "woke" a charter is by searching the student handbook for eight terms-- (1) diversity, (2) equity, (3) inclusion, (4) justice, (5) restorative, (6) social-emotional learning, (7) gender identity, and (8) culturally affirming.

And to compare these wokeness scores to the public schools and thereby prove their thesis that charters offer a wokeness respite, they... wait a minute. Hold on. No, they didn't gather any data about public schools at all.

Eight key words are a terrible way to grab a wokeness score (though I suppose it helps if, like the authors, you never really try to define the term "woke"). Assertions are not facts or data, and other articles produced by your colleagues in the same camp are not research.
It's an op-ed in search of a newspaper, though I expect it will find its way there in some form, because mostly this is just an argument to reduce regulation and promote charter schools.
